structure.title: Books I–II · Choosing a life's work
structure.text: Dorothea Brooke believes that marrying a scholar will let her take part in a great intellectual undertaking. Tertius Lydgate arrives with plans to reform medicine. Both have sincere ambitions and startlingly little curiosity about how their plans look to the people they hope will live with them.

structure.title: Books III–IV · Promises made on credit
structure.text: Fred Vincy counts on coming into money. The person who signs for a debt must answer for that confidence when the bill arrives. Courtship and professional ambition draw different households into the same network of expectations, favours and small-town news.

structure.title: Books V–VI · What the dead can still arrange
structure.text: A will can direct the living people's conduct more efficiently than its maker ever managed in person. Elsewhere a new household discovers the cost of keeping up appearances. A set of expensive objects can embody two quite different ideas of what husband and wife promised each other.

structure.title: Books VII–VIII and Finale · The town passes judgment
structure.text: Information travels between apparently separate plots until the reputation of one man can threaten the livelihood of another. Eliot follows public accusations into rooms where somebody must decide whether to make a visit, ask an embarrassing question or accept the town's verdict as sufficient.

people.name: Dorothea and Casaubon
people.text: Dorothea mistakes the difficulty of his research for evidence of its importance. Casaubon imagines a young wife will understand his need for assistance without disturbing his habits. Each has chosen the other partly for work neither can discuss with much freedom.

people.name: Lydgate and Rosamond Vincy
people.text: He reads her cultivated manners as a promise of domestic ease. She reads his origins and ambition as a promise of release from provincial life. Both impressions are made from real information. Each leaves out something the other values more than ease.

people.name: Mary Garth and Fred Vincy
people.text: Fred can afford to wait for money and purpose. Mary's household knows who does the labour while a young gentleman waits. Her affection gives her excellent grounds for declining to let him confuse her patience with permission.

context.title: Reform requires local money
context.text: Lydgate's ambitions need a hospital, patients, instruments and a patron. Decisions he experiences as medical can look commercial or political to the townspeople whose support he needs. Eliot places a professional ideal within walking distance of everybody who can obstruct it.

context.title: Saint Theresa in a provincial town
context.text: The Prelude remembers a girl who set off to become a martyr and later founded religious houses. Dorothea has a comparable appetite for serious work and no institution waiting to employ it. Designing cottages for tenants and making notes for a scholar look like two practicable ways to begin.

notice.text: Wait for the change of chair.
notice.why: Eliot can let us share a young wife's disappointment and then cross to the husband she finds unbearable. The new point of view does not undo what he has done. It lets us watch him dread an injury she scarcely knows she can inflict.

passages.quote: Was her point of view the only possible one with regard to this marriage?

notice.text: Ask whose name stands on the paper.
notice.why: Signatures on notes and conditions in wills make one household answer for another's desires. An abstract idea about character becomes a much more difficult judgment once a particular family must find the money.

opening: Dorothea wants a life devoted to something larger than herself and thinks marriage to a learned man will provide it. Lydgate arrives in town intending to transform medicine, confident that ordinary provincial compromises will not catch him. Both have admirable ambitions and incomplete knowledge of the people they need. George Eliot follows their hopes into marriages, debts, gossip, and daily negotiations, giving the supporting characters lives substantial enough to overturn a simple explanation of why someone else's future has gone wrong.
